title.en: St George and the Dragon of Silene

region.zh: 利比亞西勒尼城（傳說定位）

texts.period: The Golden Legend, compiled c. 1260 (Caxton trans., ed. Ellis, 1900)

source.work: The Golden Legend, The Life of S. George (Caxton, 1483)

summary.en: The Golden Legend's most famous episode: a pond-dragon poisons the country until children are drawn by lot, and the king's own daughter is led out as a bride for the beast; George, armed and garnished with the sign of the cross, spears and throws it down, binds it with the princess's girdle so it follows 'as it had been a meek beast', and the dragon is slain only after fifteen thousand are baptized. The canonical dragon-slayer myth of the West, told here from the hagiography that fixed its shape.
summary.zh: 《黃金傳說》最著名的一章：池中毒龍為害全境，抽籤獻童男童女，連國王之女也被裝扮如新娘送與獸；聖佐治畫十字記號、提槍刺龍並擊倒之，以公主腰帶縛龍，使其「如馴良之獸」相隨；待一萬五千人受洗後方斬龍首。西方屠龍英雄神話的原型，定型於此部聖徒傳。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition of high devotion (St George); the dragon tale is told as the tradition's own legend, with the apocryphal status the Legend itself admits noted.

passages.text: S. George was a knight and born in Cappadocia. On a time he came in to the province of Libya, to a city which is said Silene. And by this city was a stagne or a pond like a sea, wherein was a dragon which envenomed all the country. And on a time the people were assembled for to slay him, and when they saw him they fled. And when he came nigh the city he venomed the people with his breath, and therefore the people of the city gave to him every day two sheep for to feed him, because he should do no harm to the people, and when the sheep failed there was taken a man and a sheep. Then was an ordinance made in the town that there should be taken the children and young people of them of the town by lot. So it happed that many of them of the town were then delivered, insomuch that the lot fell upon the king's daughter.

When she was there S. George passed by, and when he saw the lady he demanded the lady what she made there and she said: Go ye your way fair young man, that ye perish not also. Then said he: Tell to me what have ye and why weep ye, and doubt ye of nothing. Then said S. George: Fair daughter, doubt ye no thing hereof for I shall help thee in the name of Jesu Christ. Thus as they spake together the dragon appeared and came running to them, and S. George was upon his horse, and drew out his sword and garnished him with the sign of the cross, and rode hardily against the dragon which came towards him, and smote him with his spear and hurt him sore and threw him to the ground. And after said to the maid: Deliver to me your girdle, and bind it about the neck of the dragon and be not afeard. When she had done so the dragon followed her as it had been a meek beast and debonair.

Then she led him into the city, and the people fled by mountains and valleys, and said: Alas! alas! we shall be all dead. Then S. George said to them: Ne doubt ye no thing, without more, believe ye in God, Jesu Christ, and do ye to be baptized and I shall slay the dragon. Then the king was baptized and all his people, and S. George slew the dragon and smote off his head, and commanded that he should be thrown in the fields, and they took four carts with oxen that drew him out of the city. Then were there well fifteen thousand men baptized, without women and children, and the king did do make a church there of our Lady and of S. George, in the which yet sourdeth a fountain of living water, which healeth sick people that drink thereof.

title.en: St Nicholas and the Three Masses of Gold

region.zh: 呂基亞帕塔拉（傳說定位）

texts.period: The Golden Legend, compiled c. 1260 (Caxton trans., ed. Ellis, 1900)

source.work: The Golden Legend, The Life of S. Nicholas (Caxton, 1483)

summary.en: The seed-story of Christmas's secret giver: a nobleman, impoverished, resolves to put his three virgin daughters 'to the sin of lechery so that by the gain and winning of their infamy they might be sustained' — and Nicholas, horrified, throws a mass of gold by night into the house; a second and a doubled third follow, the third witnessed as the father runs him down. The dowry-giver becomes bishop of Myra by a matins vision, and his posthumous rescue of shipwrecked mariners founds the sailor's patronage.
summary.zh: 聖誕秘密贈禮的種子故事：一位貧困貴人決意讓三個女兒「淪為娼妓以茍活」；尼古拉聞之震駭，夜間拋入一袋黃金，繼而再拋，第三次加倍——父親循聲追趕，認出聖尼古拉。憑晨禱異象他被立為米拉主教；身後顯聖拯救沉船水手，奠下海員主保之位。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition of high devotion (Santa Claus's origin); the lechery plot is the legend's own moral frame.

passages.text: And it was so that one, his neighbour, had then three daughters, virgins, and he was a nobleman: but for the poverty of them together, they were constrained, and in very purpose to abandon them to the sin of lechery, so that by the gain and winning of their infamy they might be sustained. And when the holy man Nicholas knew hereof he had great horror of this villainy, and threw by night secretly into the house of the man a mass of gold wrapped in a cloth. And when the man arose in the morning, he found this mass of gold, and rendered to God therefor great thankings, and therewith he married his oldest daughter.

And after a few days Nicholas doubled the mass of gold, and cast it into the house of this man. He awoke by the sound of the gold, and followed Nicholas, which fled from him, and he said to him: Sir, flee not away so but that I may see and know thee. Then he ran after him more hastily, and knew that it was Nicholas; and anon he kneeled down, and would have kissed his feet, but the holy man would not, but required him not to tell nor discover this thing as long as he lived.

And there was, among the others, a bishop of great authority, and all the election was in him. And when he had warned all for to be in fastings and in prayers, this bishop heard that night a voice which said to him that, at the hour of matins, he should take heed to the doors of the church, and him that should come first to the church, and have the name of Nicholas they should sacre him bishop. And this was a marvellous thing, for at the hour of matins, like as he had been sent from God, Nicholas arose tofore all other. And the bishop took him when he was come and demanded of him his name. And he, which was simple as a dove, inclined his head, and said: I have to name Nicholas.

title.en: St Ursula and the Eleven Thousand Virgins
title.zh: 聖烏蘇拉與一萬一千處女

region.en: Britannia to Cologne, pilgrimage route (legendary pin at Cologne)
region.zh: 不列顛至科隆的朝聖之路（傳說定位於科隆）

texts.period: The Golden Legend, compiled c. 1260 (Caxton trans., ed. Ellis, 1900)

source.work: The Golden Legend, The Story of S. Ursula and the Virgins (Caxton, 1483)

summary.en: The most numerically extravagant of all virgin-martyr legends: the Christian princess Ursula bargains a three-year delay of her marriage to the pagan prince of England for eleven thousand companions and his baptism; the pilgrimage fleet sails the seas, is martyred by the Huns at Cologne by an angel's prophecy, and the city's very walls are said to be built of the martyrs' bones. Cologne's ring of bones remains the story's long shadow.
summary.zh: 數目最誇張的處女殉道傳說：基督徒公主烏蘇拉以三年之期、一萬一千同伴與異教王子受洗為條件允婚；朝聖艦隊揚帆渡海，依天使預言在科隆被匈奴人所害；傳說科隆城牆竟以殉道者骸骨砌成。今日科隆的骨骸環仍是此故事的長影。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition (Cologne cult); the eleven-thousand figure is a medieval scribal legend (often read as 'undecim millia' miscopied), noted here.

passages.text: Then the king of England which then was right mighty, and subdued many nations to his empire, heard the renomee of her, and said that he would be well happy if this virgin might be coupled to his son by marriage. And there was a solemn embassy to the father of Ursula, and promised great promises, and said many fair words for to have her; and also made many menaces if they returned vainly to their lord. And she, that was divinely inspired, did so much to her father that she consented to the marriage by such a condition, that for to solace her he should send to her father ten virgins, and to herself, and to those ten other virgins, he should send to each a thousand virgins, and should give to her space of three years for to dedicate her virginity, and the young man should be baptized.

Then virgins came from all parts, and men came for to see this great company, and many bishops came for to go with them in their pilgrimage, among whom was Pantulus, bishop of Basle, which went with them to Rome, and returned from thence with them and received martyrdom. S. Gerasine, queen of Sicily, which had made of her husband that was a cruel tyrant a meek lamb, and was sister of Maurice the bishop, and of Daria, mother of S. Ursula... She, by the inspiration of God, put herself in the way with her four daughters.

title.en: St Cecilia's Angel and the Crowns of Roses and Lilies
title.zh: 聖西西里亞的天使與薔薇百合之冠

texts.period: The Golden Legend, compiled c. 1260 (Caxton trans., ed. Ellis, 1900)

source.work: The Golden Legend, The Life of S. Cecilia (Caxton, 1483)

summary.en: The making of music's patron saint: on her wedding night, hearing the organs, Cecilia sang in her heart only to God that her heart and body be kept undefiled; she warns her bridegroom Valerian of the angel guarding her — 'if he may find that ye touch my body by villainy... he shall anon slay you' — and sends him to Pope Urban at the Via Appia. Baptized, Valerian returns to find her speaking with an angel, who crowns them with roses and lilies 'which shall never fade, ne wither'.
summary.zh: 音樂主保聖女的緣起：新婚之夜，西西里亞聞風琴之聲，心裏只向神歌唱，願心身無玷；她警告新郎瓦勒良：守護她的天使若見他以穢情近她身，必立殺之——並遣他往亞比亞大道見烏爾班教宗。瓦勒良受洗歸來，見她正與天使交談；天使以永不凋謝的薔薇與百合之冠加於二人。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition (patroness of music); the chaste-marriage tale type is her legend's core.

passages.text: S. Cecilia, the holy virgin, was come of the noble lineage of the Romans, and from the time that she lay in her cradle she was fostered and nourished in the faith of Christ, and always bare in her breast the gospel hid, and never ceased day ne night from holy prayers, but recommended to God always her virginity. And when this blessed virgin should be espoused to a young man named Valerian, and the day of the wedding was come, she was clad in royal clothes of gold, but under she ware the hair. And she hearing the organs making melody, she sang in her heart, only to God, saying: O Lord, I beseech thee that mine heart and body may be undefouled so that I be not confounded.

And when they were both in their chamber alone, she said to him in this manner: O, my best beloved and sweet husband, I have a counsel to tell thee, if so be that thou wilt keep it secret and swear that ye shall bewray it to no man. I have an angel that loveth me, which ever keepeth my body whether I sleep or wake, and if he may find that ye touch my body by villainy, or foul and polluted love, certainly he shall anon slay you, and so should ye lose the flower of your youth. Then Valerian, corrected by the will of God, having dread, said to her: If thou wilt that I believe that thou sayest to me, show to me that angel that thou speakest of.

Then Valerian received baptism of S. Urban and returned home to S. Cecilia, whom he found within her chamber speaking with an angel. And this angel had two crowns of roses and lilies which he held in his hands, of which he gave one to Cecilia, and that other to Valerian, saying: Keep ye these crowns with an undefouled and clean body, for I have brought them to you from Paradise, and they shall never fade, ne wither, ne lose their savour.

title.en: St Francis and the Leper: Repair My House
title.zh: 聖方濟與痲瘋病者：修復我的聖堂

texts.period: The Golden Legend, compiled c. 1260 (Caxton trans., ed. Ellis, 1900)

source.work: The Golden Legend, The Life of S. Francis (Caxton, 1483)

summary.en: The Golden Legend's Francis: the young merchant who begs among the poor before St Peter's, runs to embrace and kiss the leper 'whom naturally men abhor' — who vanishes — and hears from the crucifix of S. Damiano: 'Francis, go and repair my house which is all destroyed as thou seest.' Selling all he had, resigning his very clothes to his father, he rebuilds the church in poverty; he preached to birds who would not flee his hand, called every beast his brother, and signed his letters with the Tau.
summary.zh: 《黃金傳說》中的方濟：少年商人赤身混入乞兒之中；奔向眾人所惡的痲瘋病者擁抱親吻——病者隨即消失——並在聖達米亞諾堂聽見十架苦像說話：「方濟，去修復我的聖堂，你看它已被破壞殆盡。」他變賣一切、把衣物交還父親，赤貧重建聖堂；向飛鳥講道，鳥不離其手；稱一切走獸為兄弟；以「陶」字印為書信之記。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition of high devotion (Franciscans); presented as hagiography.

passages.text: Francis, servant and friend of Almighty God, was born in the city of Assisi, and was made a merchant unto the twenty-fifth year of his age, and wasted his time by living vainly, whom our Lord corrected by the scourge of sickness, and suddenly changed him into another man, so that he began to shine by the spirit of prophecy.

On a time he met a leper whom naturally men abhor, but he remembered him of the word that was said of God, and ran to him and kissed him, and anon the lazar vanished away, wherefore he went to the habitation of the lazars and kissed devoutly their hands, and gave to them money, and let them have no need of such as he might do. On a time he entered into the church of S. Damian for to make his prayers, and the image of Jesu Christ spake unto him and said: Francis, go and repair my house which is all destroyed as thou seest. And from that hour the soul of him liquefied, and the passion of Jesu Christ was marvellously infixed in his heart.

The blessed S. Francis full of right great simplicity admonished and warned all creatures to love their creator. He preached to birds and was heard of them, they suffered him to touch them, and without licence they would not return ne flee from him. And on a time when he preached, the swallows chittered and sang, and anon by his commandment they were still. He spared to touch lights, lamps, and candles, because he would not defile them with his hands. He gathered the small worms out of the way because they should not be trodden with the feet of them that passed by. He called all beasts his brethren. He was replenished of marvellous joy for the love of his Creator.

title.en: Joseph of Arimathea and King Evelake's Shield
title.zh: 亞利馬太的約瑟與伊維拉克王之盾

region.en: Sarras to Great Britain (legendary pin at Glastonbury)
region.zh: 薩拉斯至大不列顛（傳說定位於格拉斯頓伯里）

source.work: Le Morte d'Arthur, Sir Thomas Malory, book XVII, chap. 10

summary.en: Malory's frame for the Grail: thirty-two years after the Passion, Joseph of Arimathea, who took down the Lord from the Cross, departs Jerusalem with his kindred for the city of Sarras, where King Evelake wars against the Saracens; taught the faith of the Trinity, Evelake has the white shield made 'in the name of Him that died upon the Cross', and in battle a cloth drawn from it reveals 'a figure of a man on the Cross', discomfiting the enemy. Evelake is baptized, follows Joseph to Great Britain — where the Grail-king is imprisoned by a felon paynim and the land turned to the Christian faith.
summary.zh: 馬洛里為聖杯所立的框架：受難後三十二年，把主從十架上放下的約瑟率親族離耶路撒冷至薩拉斯城；其地伊維拉克王正與薩拉森人交戰，聞聖三信仰後命人以「為十架受死者之名」製白盾；臨陣揭去覆布，盾上顯出「十架上人形」，敵軍潰散。伊維拉克受洗，隨約瑟至大不列顛——聖杯之王遭異邦暴君囚禁，其地全境皈依基督教。

sensitivity.note: Arthurian Christian legend; the Glastonbury pin is the traditional Joseph-in-Britain site, not historical.

passages.text: Sir Galahad, said the squire, that knight that wounded Bagdemagus sendeth you greeting, and bade that ye should bear this shield, wherethrough great adventures should befall. Then within a while came Galahad thereas the White Knight abode him by the hermitage, and everych saluted other courteously. Sir, said the knight, it befell after the passion of our Lord Jesu Christ thirty-two year, that Joseph of Aramathie, the gentle knight, the which took down our Lord off the holy Cross, at that time he departed from Jerusalem with a great party of his kindred with him. And so he laboured till that they came to a city that hight Sarras.

Then Joseph, the son of Joseph of Aramathie, went to King Evelake and told him he should be discomfit and slain, but if he left his belief of the old law and believed upon the new law. And then there he shewed him the right belief of the Holy Trinity, to the which he agreed unto with all his heart; and there this shield was made for King Evelake, in the name of Him that died upon the Cross. And then through his good belief he had the better of King Tolleme. For when Evelake was in the battle there was a cloth set afore the shield, and when he was in the greatest peril he let put away the cloth, and then his enemies saw a figure of a man on the Cross, wherethrough they all were discomfit.

Then soon after there fell a great marvel, that the cross of the shield at one time vanished away that no man wist where it became. And then King Evelake was baptised, and for the most part all the people of that city. So, soon after Joseph would depart, and King Evelake would go with him, whether he wold or nold. And so by fortune they came into this land, that at that time was called Great Britain; and there they found a great felon paynim, that put Joseph into prison. And after that all the people were turned to the Christian faith.

title.en: Christ at the Grail Table: The Child and the Bleeding Spear
title.zh: 聖杯席上的基督：聖嬰與滲血之矛

region.en: The Grail castle, realm of Logris (vision-setting)
region.zh: 聖杯城堡，洛格里斯王國（異象之境）

source.work: Le Morte d'Arthur, Sir Thomas Malory, book XVII, chap. 20

summary.en: The Grail feast as vision: four angels bear up a bishop 'in likeness of a bishop' whose forehead letters name Joseph, first bishop of Christendom; two bear candles, one a towel, one the spear that bleeds, its three drops falling into a box. At the sacring, 'there came a figure in likeness of a child, and the visage was as red and as bright as any fire, and smote himself into the bread, so that they all saw it that the bread was formed of a fleshly man' — and then a man with all the signs of the passion comes out of the Holy Vessel and feeds each knight, promising the open sight at Sarras.
summary.zh: 聖杯盛宴如異象：四位天使抬上一位額書「約瑟，基督首位主教」的主教形像；二持蠟燭、一持帕、一持滲血之矛，血滴三落於盒。行聖祭時，「一位火紅面容的嬰孩形像躍入餅中，使餅化為血肉之身」；隨後一位滿身受難印記之人自聖杯中出，親自餵養眾騎士，並許在薩拉斯城得見更敞開的異象。

sensitivity.note: Arthurian Christian legend; the Grail mass is a eucharistic vision, not a claim about the sacrament.

passages.text: Then King Pelles and his son departed. And therewithal beseemed them that there came a man, and four angels from heaven, clothed in likeness of a bishop, and had a cross in his hand; and these four angels bare him up in a chair, and set him down before the table of silver where upon the Sangreal was; and it seemed that he had in midst of his forehead letters the which said: See ye here Joseph, the first bishop of Christendom, the same which Our Lord succoured in the city of Sarras in the spiritual place. Then the knights marvelled, for that bishop was dead more than three hundred year to-fore. O knights, said he, marvel not, for I was sometime an earthly man.

And then he took an ubblie which was made in likeness of bread. And at the lifting up there came a figure in likeness of a child, and the visage was as red and as bright as any fire, and smote himself into the bread, so that they all saw it that the bread was formed of a fleshly man; and then he put it into the Holy Vessel again, and then he did that longed to a priest to do to a mass. And then he went to Galahad and kissed him, and bade him go and kiss his fellows: and so he did anon. Now, said he, servants of Jesu Christ, ye shall be fed afore this table with sweet meats that never knights tasted.

Then looked they and saw a man come out of the Holy Vessel, that had all the signs of the passion of Jesu Christ, bleeding all openly, and said: My knights, and my servants, and my true children, which be come out of deadly life into spiritual life, I will now no longer hide me from you, but ye shall see now a part of my secrets and of my hidden things: now hold and receive the high meat which ye have so much desired. Then took he himself the Holy Vessel and came to Galahad; and he kneeled down, and there he received his Saviour, and after him so received all his fellows; and they thought it so sweet that it was marvellous to tell.

title.en: Galahad King of Sarras and the Taking Up of the Grail
title.zh: 薩拉斯王加拉哈德與聖杯升天

region.en: City of Sarras, in the parts of Babylon (legendary pin)
region.zh: 薩拉斯城，巴比倫之地（傳說定位）

source.work: Le Morte d'Arthur, Sir Thomas Malory, book XVII, chaps. 21-23

summary.en: The Quest's end: a voice bids the three knights choose the youngest for king; Galahad is crowned at Sarras, where the crooked old man he summons to bear the silver table walks whole, and the tyrant Estorause's imprisoned knights are fed daily by the Grail. On the year's day Galahad asks and is given the death of his body — 'thou shalt find the life of the soul' — prays before the table, 'and then suddenly his soul departed to Jesu Christ, and a great multitude of angels bare his soul up to heaven'; a hand from heaven takes the Vessel and the spear, and sithen was there never man so hardy to say that he had seen the Sangreal.
summary.zh: 追尋的終局：有聲音命三騎士立最年少者為王；加拉哈德於薩拉斯加冕——他召來的跛足老人竟健步如初；暴君埃斯托勞斯下獄的三騎士每日蒙聖杯供養。週年之日，加拉哈德求得肉身之死——「你必得靈魂之生」——他在銀桌前禱告，「靈魂忽然離體歸於基督，眾天使攜其魂上天」；一隻自天而降的手取走聖杯與矛——「自此再無人敢言曾見聖杯」。

sensitivity.note: Arthurian Christian legend; the mystical death at prayer is the Grail cycle's eschatological apex.

passages.text: So they made Galahad king by all the assent of the holy city, and else they would have slain him. And when he was come to behold the land, he let make above the table of silver a chest of gold and of precious stones, that hilled the Holy Vessel. And every day early the three fellows would come afore it, and make their prayers. Then Galahad prayed to Our Lord that at the year's end he might pass out of this world. And so the year passed, and the self day after Galahad had prayed the prayer he was heard.

That shall I tell you, said Galahad; the other day when we saw a part of the adventures of the Sangreal I was in such a joy of heart, that I trow never man was that was earthly. And therefore I wot well, when my body is dead my soul shall be in great joy to see the blessed Trinity every day, and the majesty of Our Lord, Jesu Christ. And therewith he kneeled down to-fore the table and made his prayers, and then suddenly his soul departed to Jesu Christ, and a great multitude of angels bare his soul up to heaven, that the two fellows might well behold it.

Also the two fellows saw come from heaven an hand, but they saw not the body. And then it came right to the Vessel, and took it and the spear, and so bare it up to heaven. Sithen was there never man so hardy to say that he had seen the Sangreal. When Percivale and Bors saw Galahad dead they made as much sorrow as ever did two men. And if they had not been good men they might lightly have fallen in despair. And then he was buried; and as soon as he was buried Sir Percivale yielded him to an hermitage out of the city, and took a religious clothing.
